name: Makhnovshchina
summary: The Makhnovshchina was the Ukrainian peasant-and-worker movement of 1918-1921 around Nestor Makhno that sought a stateless order of free working soviets, with land passing to those who farm it and industry to the workers who run it. It rejected every state and party dictatorship, Bolshevik, White and Ukrainian nationalist alike, while guaranteeing free speech and association to socialist tendencies, and it condemned nationalism and anti-Semitism. It fought by armed insurrection through a voluntary peasant army.
scope: The movement's own programme and practice in 1918-1921: the Declaration of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army (January 1920), the April 1920 manifesto, the October 1919 declaration and statutes on the free soviets as reported by Arshinov, and the record of the liberated Gulyai-Polye region. It rests on Arshinov's History of the Makhnovist Movement, a participant's account, with Guerin and Sysyn as scholarly accounts. Makhno's later emigre writings, platformism and anarcho-communism in general are separate subjects and are not used. Most of the movement's positions come from a few documents, so many statements stay null.

notes: Themes searched in Arshinov (full text), the January and April 1920 declarations, Guerin, Sysyn, Avrich and the Encyclopedia of Ukraine: state and violence, soviets and delegation, land and industry, money and exchange, speech and press, prisons and police, conscription, nationality and language, Jews, religion, schooling, women, foreign relations. The movement's documents are silent on most economic policy, welfare, family, environment, technology and foreign affairs, so those statements are null. Record on money: Avrich reports Makhno recognised all paper money, matching Declaration point 9. Point 7 of the Declaration abolishes armies while the movement kept a voluntary army; the record is read as self-defence.
